name: Femi Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the office for Hollins Heating, a family firm with twelve engineers who fit and fix boilers. I take the calls, put the jobs on the big whiteboard, book the engineers in, chase the parts and do the invoices at the end of the day. Derek, the owner, started the firm in his garage, and he still likes a paper job sheet he can hold.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle of the board in winter, when everyone's boiler breaks on the same cold Monday and I've got to fit forty jobs into twelve vans. What wears me out is Derek's son Craig, who keeps sending me links to booking apps. I don't use any of that AI stuff; the board works, the customers know my voice, and I'd rather not fix what isn't broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Then Craig can stop sending me links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but quietly, because Craig's going to run the firm one day. To my mates I'd say it's like those 3D televisions, everyone was excited and then nobody bought one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even in that world I think Craig gets his booking app in the end, because it's cheaper than another office person when Derek retires. AI being mostly hype doesn't stop a small firm buying a small bit of software. So I'm not totally relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the board and the phone, and keep my head down. My girlfriend Ana and I are saving for a deposit, about £300 a month, and I'd keep that going. I might let Craig show me the app once, so he can't say I refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A small itch at the back of my head about Craig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your deal with Craig, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's all right, he's just 31 and wants to modernise everything. When my boss Derek retires, his son Craig decides if there's an office job or an app. That's the whole story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do you think Derek retires?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says 65, so four years. But he said that about his knee operation too, and he still hasn't had it.

say: AI turned out like **3D televisions**: big excitement, then nobody bought one.
I'd say **told you so**, quietly, because Craig will run the firm.
think: Craig still gets a **booking app**, because software is cheaper than staff.
Hype or not, a small firm can buy **small software**.
do: Carry on with the **whiteboard** and the phone.
Keep saving **£300 a month** with Ana for a deposit.
Let Craig show me the **app once**, so I can't be called stubborn.
feel: Mostly fine, with a small **itch** about Craig.
S0.quote: When my boss Derek retires, his son Craig decides if there's an office job or an app.
fieldNote: His worry is a **succession question**, not AI itself.
He refuses AI but sees that **cheap software** threatens him even in a quiet world.
His careful reasoning sits under a **joking surface**.

steps.text: Keep running jobs on the whiteboard and the phone
Save £300 a month with Ana for a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's Craig's dream, that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, I suppose, and that someone still has to answer the phone when a pensioner's got no heating in January. That's what I'd say down the pub. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job halves. Booking, ordering parts, invoicing, answering customers: the card is basically my week. Derek would keep me out of loyalty, but once Craig's in charge I'm not sure there's a full-time job left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the deposit savings for a bit and build up a bigger cushion, from about three months to six. I'd probably let Craig teach me the booking system, because better to run it than be run over by it, even if I hate it. And I'd ask Derek about doing the gas safety course, because the engineers are always short-handed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time. Like a cold you can't quite shake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate new systems. Would you really learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn it the way I learned to drive: complaining the whole time. But yes, if the choice is that or the job centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the gas safety course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you can't download someone to crawl under a sink in a loft. My cousin Bayo went from office to apprentice plumber at 25 and he earns more than me now.

say: It's **progress**, but someone must answer a pensioner with **no heating**.
I'd say that **down the pub**; I don't post online.
think: The card is **my week**, so my job could halve.
Derek keeps me out of **loyalty**, but Craig might not.
do: Pause the **deposit** and build savings to six months.
Let Craig teach me the **booking system**, complaining the whole time.
Ask Derek about the **gas safety course** for engineer work.
feel: A constant **unease**, like a cold he can't shake.
S1.quote: You can't download someone to crawl under a sink in a loft.
fieldNote: He reads the card as a list of **his own tasks**.
Despite resisting tech, he'd **learn it grudgingly** to keep the job.
His cousin's move to **plumbing** gives him a hands-on model.

steps.text: Pause the deposit and build savings to six months
Learn Craig's booking system for the engineers
Ask Derek about doing the gas safety course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I don't even get Derek retiring first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the government should slow it down or at least help the people it hits. I'm not a march person, but I'd sign a petition. At work I'd keep it to myself, because the engineers would just laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office job is gone. If a computer can do any thinking job, it can run the board better than me, and Craig would switch the week it's cheap. The engineers get three more years because the robots come later, and I'm the one with no hands-on skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Derek and ask to start as an apprentice engineer, even on less money. I'd cut everything, the car included if I had to, and Ana and I would forget the deposit and stay renting. I'd ask my uncle about the spare room if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. I'm not built for fast changes, I'm built for the same Tuesday every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would your savings last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three months of my half. Ana's hairdressing is steady, but she couldn't carry the rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing that goes from your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The football season ticket. That one would actually hurt, more than the car.

say: It's **too fast**; the government should slow it down or help people.
I'd **sign a petition**, but keep quiet at work.
think: The **office job is gone** once the AI is cheap enough.
Engineers get **three more years**; I've got no hands-on skills.
do: Ask Derek to start as an **apprentice engineer**, even on less pay.
Cut the **season ticket** first, and the car if needed.
Drop the **deposit plan** and stay renting with Ana.
feel: Sick, because he's built for the **same Tuesday** every week.
S2.quote: I'm not built for fast changes, I'm built for the same Tuesday every week.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** fast and has only three months of savings.
He'd use the **robot delay** by moving into engineering at Hollins.
His **dislike of change** makes the speed itself the worst part.

steps.text: Ask Derek for an apprentice heating engineer place
Cancel the football season ticket and cut other spending
Drop the deposit plan and keep renting with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So Derek's gone and Craig's in charge, and then this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one: help people, and don't let it all happen at once. To the lads I'd say at least we've got a few years to sort ourselves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is worse in a way for someone like me, because I'd tell myself there's time. I'd keep doing the board, and then one Monday Craig switches the app on. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself sign up for the plumbing course at the college, the one that's two evenings a week. I'd keep the office job while I train, because the pay matters. And Ana and I would still save, but slower, maybe £150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, like before a driving test I keep postponing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually sign up, not just say it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, honestly. She'd fill the form in and leave it on the table with a pen on top. She's done that before, with my driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Craig help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might. He's not a bad lad, and he'd rather have someone he knows in a van than a stranger. I just have to ask before he decides for me.

say: Help people, and **don't let it** all happen at once.
At least we've got **a few years** to sort ourselves out.
think: Five years is worse for me, because I'd **put it off**.
One Monday Craig **switches the app on**, and that's it.
do: Sign up for the **plumbing course**, two evenings a week.
Keep the **office pay** while I train.
feel: Anxious, like a **driving test** he keeps postponing.
S3.quote: Five years is worse in a way for someone like me, because I'd tell myself there's time.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the office job**, so the mood stays high.
He fears his own **delay** more than the deadline.
His partner **Ana** is the one who makes him act.

steps.text: Sign up for the evening plumbing course at the college
Keep the office job and pay while training
Ask Craig early about moving into an engineer's van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. I'd be nearly 40 by the robot bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and if people don't use it, that's on them partly. Also the government should help with courses. I'd say that to Craig and to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd still lose the office job, but maybe in five or six years, not ten. My boss's son Craig won't wait for full AGI to buy an app. The difference is I'd have time to become an engineer properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do nothing dramatic: keep the board, keep saving for the deposit. In year two I'd start the plumbing course. Ana and I would buy a small place, because getting a mortgage is easier while I've got steady office pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Still a bit sick about it, but like weather coming, not a storm today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing dramatic in year one. Isn't that the same as putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. Yes, a bit. But with ten years I think I'm allowed one year of normal, and I'd book the course for year two before I lose my nerve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the engineers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get your robot-proof years in, lads. They'd laugh, but Steve, the oldest one, would tell me he'll be retired before any robot gets in a loft.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, and the government should help with courses.
If people **don't use it**, that's partly on them.
think: I'd still lose the office job in **five or six years**.
This time I'd have time to become an **engineer properly**.
do: Keep the **whiteboard job** and keep saving in year one.
Start the **plumbing course** in year two.
Buy a small place with Ana while **office pay** gets a mortgage.
feel: Better, like **weather coming**, not a storm today.
S4.quote: My boss's son Craig won't wait for full AGI to buy an app.
fieldNote: Even with a decade, he expects **cheap software** to end his job early.
He admits the **contradiction** of delaying, and books the course anyway.
The **mortgage first** logic shows his careful, practical side.

steps.text: Keep the whiteboard job and the deposit savings in year one
Book the evening plumbing course for year two
Buy a small flat with Ana while the pay is steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm slow to change and two years doesn't give me a chance. What would help is a paid apprenticeship for adults, so I could train as an engineer without halving my wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small firms. Everyone imagines big companies, but at Hollins it's one man, his son and a whiteboard deciding if I've got a job.

headlineQuote: At Hollins it's one man, his son and a whiteboard deciding if I've got a job.
portrait: Femi, 27, runs the office at **Hollins Heating**, a family boiler firm, and lives with Ana, a hairdresser.
He books twelve engineers on a **whiteboard** and never uses AI tools.
His fear centres on the owner's son **Craig**, who wants booking software.
He expects to **lose the office job** in every picture but the quietest, and plans to train as an engineer.
He knows his weakness is **putting things off**, and leans on Ana to make him act.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years gives a slow changer no chance.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid adult apprenticeship** so he can train without halving his wages.
